item.content:encoded:
I don't think the definition of "hook" quite lines up with how it's generally used around here.
To be sure, that is what "hook" means to the larger world, in a creative writing class for example.
But here on the wiki the term is something closer to "the thing that makes the reader care about the article".
When we advise someone in the forums that their writing "needs a hook", we generally don't mean that it needs more early reader engagement. We mean that it needs a unique twist, unexpected wrinkle, novel spin, etc. that will make the reader feel like their time wasn't wasted after they are done reading.

SCP "hook" and IRL "hook" both mean something that engages the reader; but the SCP usage is about what makes them ultimately up-vote, not about what gets them to keep reading. Or that's how I see it being used, at any rate.

item.content:encoded:
I feel the same way about this that I did about the "List of XK Events" page that popped up a while ago. It's not a bad idea to have something like this, but it's also something that should be approached with either more planning and collaboration than the usual writing-suggestions essay, or less athoritative tone and dress (e.g. the URL) than an official site guide.

As a side note, it also highlights the disjointed nature of site culture: we simultaneously explain to new contributors that there is no canon, so everyone has their own head-version of characterization and continuity, and that we as a community have very specific and rigid ideas about what the Foundation is like and what an SCP is supposed to be. These two aspects of the site are supposed to be compatible, but they come into conflict whenever someone uses the word "amnesiac".

item.content:encoded: Not quite right. "Uncontained" means that its effects aren't contained, but we can still suppress information about it. "Explained", by the example of 8900-EX, includes ones where we literally cannot prevent all of humanity from being exposed to it, so we accept it as normal. This is why Explained articles are so fundamentally difficult to write; it's such a narrow space that it's hard to write something with a degree of plausibility.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
doctor — A medical expert. Often incorrectly used in the same way as researcher; while anyone with a Ph.D may use the title "Dr.", they are generally not referred to as a "doctor" and certainly not in the context of the Foundation.

Someone with a Doctor of Philosophy is automatically awarded the title of "doctor", and it is proper to address them as such (unless they're in the military, in which case you generally call them by their rank rather than title). For example, my father is holds a PhD in physics, and is properly referred to and addressed as "Dr. Hornby" or "Professor Hornby". That said, you would refer to him as a "physicist", rather than a "doctor" (even though he has a doctorate), but you would address him neither as "Physicist Hornby" nor "Researcher Hornby".

  • IRL, I am a person who does research for a living, do not (yet) hold a terminal degree, and would be addressed as "Mr. Hornby" and called a "researcher", but not called "Researcher Hornby".
  • IRL, my father is a professor of physics (and does research in that field), holds a terminal degree in physics, and is addressed as "Dr. Hornby" or "Professor Hornby", and called a "professor" or a "physicist", but is not called a "doctor".
  • IRL, my uncle is a professor of medicine, holds a terminal degree in medicine, and is addressed as "Dr. Daniel" or "Professor Daniel", and may be called either a "professor" or a "doctor".
  • IRL, the medical doctor who I see for routine checkups holds a terminal degree in medicine, and is addressed "Dr. Smith", but since he is neither a professor nor a researcher, would not be called "Professor Smith", and would be referred to as a "doctor" but not as a "professor" nor a "researcher".

"Doctor" is both a title1 and a profession2:

  • A researcher(position) may or may not be a doctor(title), and even if that researcher is a doctor(title), that doesn't necessarily mean that s/he is a doctor(medical profession).
  • Extremely rare circumstances aside, a doctor(medical profession) is a doctor(title), since s/he has a terminal degree (an MD), but there's no guarantee that a doctor(medical profession) is a researcher(position).

This is what we get for having a language with multiple definitions per word.

Short version: Yes, the term "doctor" does get misused on the wiki. That said, the entry as written is either incomplete or wrong.

Edit: Otherwise, I generally approve of this page.

Footnotes
1. Properly reserved for those with terminal degrees in their field of study, which is generally a PhD or MD.
2. As in, a medical doctor.
